title: The Case for Lumpiness
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: As part of his ongoing series on the disciplines of "life stewardship," Dave Stuart Jr. argues that becoming an expert requires accepting uneven, "lumpy" growth rather than uniform competence across every part of the job. He first pushes back on American skepticism toward expertise, arguing that reality -- not personal will -- governs outcomes like student motivation, so teachers must apprentice themselves to fundamentals rather than assume they can simply determine their own classroom reality. He defines an expert as someone who has stayed stubbornly focused on a small set of fundamental questions long enough to develop an evidence-based toolkit, and laments that teaching's high attrition rate makes real expertise rare, producing a "blind leading the blind" dynamic in many schools. The core argument is that pursuing uniform excellence across every domain of the job (wanting every line of the teacher eval rubric to shine, chasing every trending edu-topic) actually prevents expertise, because real growth requires concentrating effort unevenly. He closes with a practical directive to eliminate any commitment or distraction not aligned with one's chosen focus area (his recurring "sled dogs" metaphor).
points: Expertise is defined narrowly as staying stubbornly focused on a small set of fundamental questions long enough to build a genuine, evidence-based toolkit -- not broad competence across every domain of the job.

High teacher attrition before the five-year mark is named as the direct cause of an expertise shortage in schools, producing a "blind leading the blind" dynamic that Stuart says causes real, unintentional harm.

The central claim is that wanting uniform excellence -- every line of the eval rubric shiny, every trending edu-topic chased -- actively prevents the uneven, concentrated effort that produces real expertise.

The practical takeaway is to eliminate commitments and distractions not aligned with one's chosen focus ("sled dogs"), treating this elimination as the price of admission for eventually reaching genuine expertise.
quotes: First, expertise is viewed with extreme (and I think, often deeply foolish) skepticism in the United States. The culture is rife with the idea that experts are outdated; we can all be our own experts; you've got to be wary of what the experts tell you; "Who made you an expert!?
An expert is just someone who has spent a large deal of time stubbornly and intelligently and sustainably focused on fundamental questions.

There is no greater prize in our own professional development than the slow and steady acquisition of expertise. But in a profession that loses most of its people before they reach five years' experience, expertise is rare. Calamitously so.
We're uncomfortable with accepting that most parts of our practice must be good enough in order for some parts of our practice to be exceptional. We don't want to be lumpy; we want to be uniform.
When a lesson doesn't go well, we head to Google or TPT, not our teacher's journals — convinced that the answer is out there, all silvery and powerful, if only we could just click the right link.
So I say, be lumpy. And start by ELIMINATING: Any commitment that you have — committee, club, team, role, seat — that's not aligned with your sled dogs.
